561.title: The rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31)
561.hook: a beggar at the gate has a name; the rich man doesn't
561.howItsDone: Christians read this parable when thinking about wealth and about those at their own gate, and some church outreach to people living on the street begins with learning names.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shrewd manager, and a warning that you cannot serve God and mammon. Your line was faithful in little. Who did you spend a little on? Day five hundred sixty-one.

The man who sells the newspaper. The woman who cleans the office after everyone goes home. Someone sitting by the same doorway each morning with a paper cup. Faces seen every day, and no names to go with them. Jesus tells a story about a gate, and two men on either side of it. Only one of them gets a name, and it isn't the one you'd expect. Some readers point out that no other character in his parables is named at all.

In the King James Bible: "There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day." Purple was the cloth of kings. This man dressed like royalty and feasted every day. "And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, which was laid at his gate, full of sores." Laid there, as if someone carried him because he couldn't walk. He longs for the crumbs from the table, and the dogs come and lick his sores. Lazarus is a Greek form of the Hebrew name Eleazar, usually explained as God has helped. Nobody else is helping him. The rich man, meanwhile, has no name at all. Later tradition called him Dives, but that's just the Latin word for rich. Both men die. Lazarus is carried by angels to Abraham's side; the rich man is in torment. And here's the detail that stings. The rich man calls across to Abraham: send Lazarus to cool my tongue. He knew his name. Every time he passed that gate, he knew exactly who was lying there. The story never says he kicked him or cursed him. He just didn't see him as someone who was his to help. Abraham answers that a great gulf is now fixed between them. The rich man begs for Lazarus to warn his five brothers. Abraham says they have Moses and the prophets. And the last line: "neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead." Christians differ on how literally to read the afterlife scenes here; some take them as a parable, not a map. Either way, the story starts at the gate. The gulf began there.
screen: then, large: `A CERTAIN BEGGAR NAMED LAZARUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn a name. Settle and breathe. Picture your ordinary route through a day: the street, the shop, the bus, the building where you work. Who do you pass, again and again, without knowing their name? The cleaner, the security guard, the man at the corner, the cashier with the tired smile. Let their faces come up one by one. Choose one. Today, or the next time you see them, ask their name, and tell them yours. If you pray, you can pray for them by name afterward. The bell holds the time.
Lazarus. The beggar at the gate, his name a Greek form of Eleazar, God has helped — the only character named in any of Jesus' parables.
Your line: the beggar had a name. Today, learn one name you should already know, and use it. Day five hundred sixty-one.

562.title: Faith like a mustard seed (Luke 17:1–10)
562.hook: the apostles ask for more faith; he says a mustard seed is enough
562.howItsDone: Some Christians pray the apostles' words, increase our faith, in times of doubt, and some churches teach that faith grows by acting on it in small daily obedience rather than waiting for certainty.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rich man and Lazarus, and a gate where a gulf began. Your line was the beggar had a name. Whose name did you learn? Day five hundred sixty-two.

I need more. More faith, more confidence, more certainty. If I just believed harder, I could do the hard thing. It's a request some people of faith know well, and Luke shows exactly when the apostles make it. Not after a storm, not in front of a miracle. Right after Jesus gives them an instruction about forgiveness that sounds, frankly, impossible. Their reply is three words in the King James Bible, and there's nothing polished about it.

Here's the instruction: if your brother wrongs you, tell him; if he repents, forgive him. "And if he trespass against thee seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turn again to thee, saying, I repent; thou shalt forgive him." Seven times in one day. Anyone who's lived with a sibling or a roommate knows how hard that is. So the apostles say: "Increase our faith." Add to it. Give us more. And Jesus doesn't. He answers: "If ye had faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye might say unto this sycamine tree, Be thou plucked up by the root, and be thou planted in the sea; and it should obey you." A mustard seed is tiny. A sycamine is a full-grown tree, rooted in the ground. Uprooting it, and planting it in the sea of all places, is a deliberately absurd picture. Readers hear this answer in more than one way. Some hear a gentle rebuke: you don't yet have even a seed's worth. Others hear encouragement: the point isn't how much faith you have, and even a speck of real trust in God is enough to do impossible things. On that reading, you don't need more before you start. Then he tells a short story that sounds harsh at first. A servant comes in from plowing, and his master doesn't say, sit down, let me serve you. The servant makes dinner first. And Jesus says, so you too, when you've done everything you were told, say: "We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do." Put the two together, and on that reading, forgiving seven times a day isn't a heroic feat that needs a giant supply of faith. It's the next job, done with a little faith, the way a servant makes dinner. No medal. Just the work, and the seed doing what seeds do.
screen: then, large: `IF YE HAD FAITH AS A GRAIN OF MUSTARD SEED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: use the faith you already have. Settle and breathe. Think of something you've been putting off until you feel more ready, more sure, more faithful. A forgiveness, an apology, a hard conversation, a step in prayer or service. Notice the voice that says not yet, I need more first. Now picture the mustard seed: small enough to lose in your palm. In the saying, that's enough to move a tree. What is the smallest first step you could take today, with what you've got? Name it. If you pray, you can say the apostles' words: increase our faith. Then take the step anyway. The bell holds the time.
Mustard seed, the tiniest seed Jesus names — asked for more faith, he says even a speck like it is enough to uproot a tree, so use what you have and do the next thing.
Your line: increase our faith. Today, take the small first step you named, before you feel ready. Day five hundred sixty-two.

563.title: Ten healed, one returned (Luke 17:11–19)
563.hook: ten lepers healed; only a Samaritan comes back to say thank you
563.howItsDone: Catholics, Orthodox Christians, Anglicans, Lutherans and others call communion the Eucharist, the thanksgiving; in the United States, some churches read the story of the ten lepers around Thanksgiving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith like a mustard seed, enough to uproot a tree. Your line was increase our faith. Did you take the small step? Day five hundred sixty-three.

Between Samaria and Galilee, at the edge of a village, ten men are standing at a distance. They have to. They have leprosy, the Bible's word for skin diseases that made a person unclean, and the law said such people must live apart. So they've lost their homes, their work, the touch of their families. Ten of them, and at least one, we'll learn, is a Samaritan. Trouble has put them all on the same road. They see Jesus coming down the road, and they don't come closer. They lift up their voices.

In the King James Bible they cry: "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us." He doesn't touch them or even say be healed. He says: "Go shew yourselves unto the priests." That's what the law required for someone who'd recovered: a priest had to confirm it. But they're not recovered yet. They have to start walking while still sick. "And it came to pass, that, as they went, they were cleansed." As they went. Somewhere along the road, they look down and the skin is clean. And then, the turn: "And one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, and with a loud voice glorified God, And fell down on his face at his feet, giving him thanks: and he was a Samaritan." The same loud voice he'd used to beg, now used to praise. Giving him thanks, in Greek, is eucharisteo. Eu, good; charis, grace or gift. It's where the word Eucharist comes from, the name Catholics, Orthodox Christians, Anglicans and others use for communion, the great thanksgiving. Jesus asks: "Were there not ten cleansed? but where are the nine?" To be fair to the nine, they were doing exactly what they were told, heading to the priests. Luke never calls them ungrateful. But only one stopped, turned around, and came back before going on. And Jesus calls him "this stranger," a foreigner. The outsider is the one who sees the gift. Then the last word: "Arise, go thy way: thy faith hath made thee whole." All ten were cleansed. Some readers notice that only this one hears that he's been made whole. The healing reached his skin. The thanks reached further.
screen: then, large: `THY FAITH HATH MADE THEE WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go back and say thank you. Settle and breathe. Think back over the last year. What good thing happened to you that you received and walked on from? A recovery, a rescue, a favor at work, someone who stood by you when they didn't have to. Picture the person who made it possible. Picture yourself turning around on the road. What would you say? Find the words now. Then decide how you'll say them: a message, a call, a note, a visit. If you pray, you can turn back to God with the same thanks. The bell holds the time.
Eucharisteo. Greek for giving thanks: good grace. What the one healed Samaritan did when he turned back, and the root of the word Eucharist.
Your line: where are the nine? Today, be the one who turns back: send the thank-you you've been meaning to send. Day five hundred sixty-three.

564.title: The kingdom among you (Luke 17:20–37)
564.hook: the kingdom of God is within you, or in your midst
564.howItsDone: Christians pray thy kingdom come every time they say the Lord's Prayer, and some churches speak of the kingdom as both already present and not yet complete, especially in Advent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ten were healed and one returned, giving thanks. Your line was where are the nine? Who did you turn back to thank? Day five hundred sixty-four.

When? Some Pharisees put the question to Jesus straight: when will the kingdom of God come? When will things be put right? When will God act? When will his reign be plain to see? Under Roman rule, people longed for that day. It's a fair question. If Jesus really is bringing it, when does it start? His answer is just two verses long, and one tiny phrase in it can be read two ways.

In the King James Bible, he says: "The kingdom of God cometh not with observation: Neither shall they say, Lo here! or, lo there! for, behold, the kingdom of God is within you." Not with observation: it isn't something you can track like an astronomer watching for a comet. Don't chase people who say it's over here, or over there. Then the tiny phrase. In Greek, entos hymon. It can mean within you, inside each person. That's how the King James reads it, and Leo Tolstoy took the title of a book from it. But it can also mean among you, in your midst. Other translations prefer that. Some readers point out that Jesus is speaking to people who were questioning him, and that the one standing in front of them was Jesus himself. On that reading, the kingdom is already here, in the middle of you, and you're asking when. Christians hold both readings. Some stress the inner life: God's reign begins in the heart. Others stress the community and the person of Jesus: God's reign is happening right here, among people, in what he's doing. Some hold the two together. Then Jesus turns to his disciples and talks about the future: a day that will come as suddenly as lightning, while people are busy eating, drinking, marrying, planting, just as in the days of Noah and of Lot. Three words of warning: "Remember Lot's wife." She looked back. The whole passage holds two things together: the kingdom is already here, close enough to touch, and it is still coming. The question was when. The answer points to where: closer than the horizon, already in the room.
screen: then, large: `THE KINGDOM OF GOD IS WITHIN YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for the kingdom in the room. Settle and breathe. Look around wherever you are. Notice the people near you, or the traces of people: a photo, a gift, the chair someone sat in. Where is there kindness here, patience, forgiveness, peace, even a small amount? Name one or two places. Then turn inward. Where in you is there something like that, a small good thing already growing? You don't have to manufacture it. Just notice it's there. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
Entos hymon, the Greek phrase that can mean within you or among you — Jesus' answer to when the kingdom comes: already here, already in the room, and still coming.
Your line: in your midst. Today, once every few hours, stop and look for one sign of the kingdom right where you are. Day five hundred sixty-four.

565.title: Of such is the kingdom (Luke 18:15–17)
565.hook: they bring even infants to be touched
565.howItsDone: Many churches baptize infants, including Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, Methodist and Reformed churches, while Baptists and many others hold services of dedication and blessing for babies and baptize those who profess faith for themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, entos hymon, the kingdom among you, already here and still coming. Your line was in your midst. Where did you spot it? Day five hundred sixty-five.

Picture a crowd around a famous teacher. Serious men with serious questions about the law, about the end of the age, about money and the kingdom. And pushing in at the edges, a group of parents carrying babies. Not toddlers who could ask questions. Babies, swaddled, asleep, maybe crying. All the parents want is for him to lay his hand on them. To the disciples, it looks like a distraction from the real work. You can almost hear them: not now, he's busy.

Matthew and Mark tell this story too, and in their versions the children are paidia, young children. Luke changes one word. In the King James Bible: "And they brought unto him also infants, that he would touch them: but when his disciples saw it, they rebuked them." Infants. In Greek, brephe, babies. It's the same word Luke used for John the Baptist leaping in Elisabeth's womb, and for Jesus himself, the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger. Luke wants us to see newborns here. And these babies can't do anything. They can't believe, or understand, or even ask to be brought. Then Jesus: "But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Suffer little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God." Suffer, in old English, means allow. Let them come. Then the line that turns it around on the adults: "Verily I say unto you, Whosoever shall not receive the kingdom of God as a little child shall in no wise enter therein." What does a baby do? It receives. It's carried, fed, held. It doesn't earn anything. Luke puts this just after the story of the tax collector who could only say God be merciful to me. The same point twice: the kingdom isn't achieved, it's received. Christians apply this in different ways. Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, Methodist and Reformed churches baptize infants, and some read this passage at baptisms. Baptists and many others dedicate babies with a blessing and baptize those old enough to profess faith themselves. Both hear the same thing in it: the youngest are not a distraction. They're the model.
screen: then, large: `FOR OF SUCH IS THE KINGDOM OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless a child. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind a child you know: your own, a grandchild, a niece, a neighbor's baby, a child you used to be. See their face. Hold them in your mind as if carrying them toward someone who loves them. Wish them good things, slowly: safety, kindness around them, room to grow. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you're with a child today, some families bless them with a hand on the head or a sign of the cross at bedtime. Or just tell them they matter. The bell holds the time.
Brephe, the Greek word for infants, newborns — the babies the disciples tried to send away, and the ones Jesus says the kingdom belongs to, received like a child.
Your line: as a little child. Today, receive one good thing without trying to earn it or pay it back. Just say thank you. Day five hundred sixty-five.

566.title: One thing you lack (Luke 18:18–30)
566.hook: a rich ruler goes away sad; Peter says we've left everything
566.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox monks and nuns, and members of some Protestant communities, take vows of poverty in response to this call, while other Christians hear it as an invitation to hold possessions loosely and give generously.

segments.voice: Yesterday, brephe, infants carried to Jesus, and the kingdom received as a little child. What did you receive without paying it back? Day five hundred sixty-six.

Straight after the babies, who can do nothing, comes a man who has done everything right. Luke calls him a certain ruler: a leader, respected, wealthy. He's not trying to trap Jesus. He seems to really want to know. And his question is the big one: "Good Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?" What shall I do. He's used to achieving things. He wants the list. Put him next to the babies from yesterday and the contrast is almost painful: the ones who can't do anything, and the one who wants to know what to do.

Jesus first pushes back on the compliment: "Why callest thou me good? none is good, save one, that is, God." Then he names commandments: don't commit adultery, don't kill, don't steal, don't bear false witness, honor your father and mother. And the man says, sincerely, "All these have I kept from my youth up." Then Jesus says: "Yet lackest thou one thing: sell all that thou hast, and distribute unto the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, follow me." One thing. Not a longer list. A single loosening of the grip. "And when he heard this, he was very sorrowful: for he was very rich." Luke doesn't say he stormed off. He doesn't even say he left. He was sad. He seems to have wanted it, and couldn't let go. Then the hard saying: it's easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God. You may have heard that there was a small gate in Jerusalem called the Needle's Eye, where camels had to kneel to get through. It's a nice sermon, but there's no ancient evidence for such a gate. Jesus seems to mean exactly what it sounds like: impossible. The listeners get it. "Who then can be saved?" And the answer that becomes today's line: "The things which are impossible with men are possible with God." Then Peter, a little anxious: "Lo, we have left all, and followed thee." And Jesus promises that no one who leaves house or family for the kingdom will miss out, now or in the age to come. Christians have read the one thing in different ways. Some take it as this man's particular call. Others, like Antony of Egypt, who heard Matthew's version read in church, took it as their own and gave everything away.
screen: then, large: `HE WAS VERY SORROWFUL: FOR HE WAS VERY RICH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name what you'd find hardest to leave. Settle and breathe. Imagine being asked, gently, for one thing. Not everything, just the thing you hold tightest. Money, a home, a reputation, a relationship, a plan for your life, a comfort you reach for every night. Notice what comes up first. Don't argue with it, and don't try to give it up right now. Just name it, honestly, the way the ruler's sorrow was honest. Then hold the line: what is impossible with men is possible with God. If you pray, you can hand that one thing over in your mind, for a moment. The bell holds the time.
One thing you lack. A rich ruler who kept every commandment hears he lacks one thing, to let go and follow, and is left very sorrowful.
Your line: what is impossible with men. Today, when you meet something you can't let go of, say the rest of the line: is possible with God. Day five hundred sixty-six.

567.title: What do you want? (Luke 18:31–43)
567.hook: a blind beggar at Jericho shouts, and Jesus stops the whole procession
567.howItsDone: Some Christians hear the blind man's cry, have mercy on me, in the Jesus Prayer that Orthodox Christians and others repeat, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me; the story is also read when praying for healing and for spiritual sight.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a rich ruler heard one thing you lack and was very sorrowful. Your line was what is impossible with men. What did you name as hardest to leave? Day five hundred sixty-seven.

Just before Jericho, Jesus takes the twelve aside and tells them plainly what's going to happen in Jerusalem: he will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, spat on, killed, and on the third day rise again. You can't say it much more plainly than that. And Luke adds a sentence that is almost sad: "And they understood none of these things: and this saying was hid from them." They have eyes. They've seen everything. And they can't see. Then, on the road outside Jericho, they meet a man who has no eyesight at all.

Luke doesn't name him; Mark calls him Bartimaeus. He's sitting by the roadside, begging, and he hears a crowd going by. What's happening? Jesus of Nazareth is passing. And he shouts, in the King James Bible: "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me." Son of David. That's a title for the promised king. The man who can't see is the one who sees who Jesus is. The people at the front of the crowd tell him to be quiet. "But he cried so much the more." Louder. And then, the line behind our carry: "And Jesus stood, and commanded him to be brought unto him." A whole crowd on the road to Jerusalem, moving, and it stops. For one beggar. Then a question that sounds almost too obvious: "What wilt thou that I shall do unto thee?" Isn't it clear? But Jesus asks anyway. He lets the man say it for himself, as a person with a voice and not just a problem. "Lord, that I may receive my sight." The Greek verb can mean see again, and it can mean look up. "And immediately he received his sight, and followed him, glorifying God." He followed him, up the road to Jerusalem, toward everything the disciples couldn't understand. Look at this week. A beggar at a gate with a name. Faith the size of a seed. One who turned back to say thank you. A kingdom in your midst. Babies carried forward. A ruler who couldn't let go. And now a blind man who could see, a shout that stopped a crowd, and a question: what do you want?
screen: `SON OF DAVID: HE SEES WHO HE IS.`
then, large: `LORD, THAT I MAY RECEIVE MY SIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop for someone shouting for help. Settle and breathe. Think about the voices around you asking for help, some loud, some quiet: a friend who keeps mentioning a hard time, a colleague who's struggling, a cause in the news, a family member who calls too often. Which one have you been walking past? Imagine stopping, the whole procession of your day halting, and asking that person: what do you want me to do for you? Then listen for their answer, not yours. If you pray, you can ask for eyes to see who's calling. The bell holds the time.
What do you want? Jesus' question to a blind beggar he stopped a whole procession for, letting him say for himself: that I may receive my sight.
Your line: Jesus stood still. Today, stop for the person you've been walking past, and ask them what they want. Day five hundred sixty-seven, and another week on the path.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle story about a blind man healed.
what it means: the blind man sees who Jesus is, shouts louder when hushed, and is asked what he wants, while the disciples with eyes understand nothing.
what a scholar hears: Luke sets the blind man straight after the disciples' failure to understand, and his son of David is a royal title on the road to Jerusalem.
